name: Victor Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do nights on a general medical ward at the district hospital, the one by the ring road. Seven at night to half seven in the morning, four nights on, four off. It's chest infections, falls, diabetics whose sugars have gone wild, and a lot of old men who want to go home at 2 a.m. I do the drug round, the obs every four hours, and I'm usually the one who catches the patient who's quietly getting worse.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about nights, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Nights are calmer in one way: no managers, no visiting, just you and the patients. I keep a little paper notebook in my top pocket with every patient's numbers, which the day staff laugh at. What wears me out is sleeping in the day, and my girlfriend Ines, who cuts hair, works Saturdays, so we barely see each other some weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, told you so. Everyone was getting excited and it turned out to be a fancy autocomplete. I wouldn't post anything, I don't really do that, but I'd say it at the nurses' station at three in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means nothing changes, and that's fine. Nurses are always needed, there are two other hospitals within half an hour, and my pay goes up on the scale every year. Ines and I are saving for a deposit on a flat, about four months' worth so far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my nights and keep saving three hundred a month for the deposit. If they bring in some routine AI charting, I'd use it only if I had to, and I'd keep my notebook anyway. That's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's what I expected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about your situation that worries you, apart from AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The deposit. Flat prices round here keep going up faster than we can save. And nights do something to your body, you know, I'm twenty-seven and I sleep like an old man.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you keep the paper notebook when there's a computer system?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the computer goes down, and when it goes down at 4 a.m. nobody comes to fix it. My notebook never crashes, and Ruth (the nurse who trained me) kept one too and never missed a deteriorating patient.

say: AI turned out to be a **fancy autocomplete**, as he expected.
He'd say it at the **nurses' station** at 3 a.m., not online.
think: Nurses are **always needed**, with two other hospitals nearby.
He and Ines have **four months** saved toward a deposit.
do: Keeps working **four nights on**, four off.
Saves **three hundred a month** for the flat deposit.
Uses any **AI charting** only if forced, keeping his paper notebook.
S0.quote: My notebook never crashes, and Ruth (the nurse who trained me) kept one too and never missed a deteriorating patient.
fieldNote: Trusts **paper over screens**, learned from his mentor Ruth.
Main worry is **house prices** outrunning his savings.
Feels secure with **two other hospitals** within half an hour.
Night shifts take a **physical toll** he mentions casually.

steps.text: Keep working four nights on, four off on the medical ward
Save three hundred a month toward the flat deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll see. A lot of these things get announced and then nobody uses them. At work I'd say, as long as it doesn't slow down the drug round, I don't care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it probably won't touch me much. Night nursing is mostly hands and eyes. What would bother me is if the hospital used the AI to cut the night healthcare assistant, because then I'd be doing washes and obs on my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the training when it's compulsory, not before. I'd keep the deposit savings going, but I might hold off buying for a year to see how jobs look. And I'd ask Ines how the salon's doing, because if her bookings go online through some AI, fewer walk-ins maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not for me so much, but the ward around me changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hold off buying the flat. Why, if your job's safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a mortgage is twenty-five years, and I don't know what twenty-five years looks like anymore. If I wait one year and nothing bad happens, I've lost nothing. Ines thinks I'm being slow, which I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say if a manager asked you to be one of the first to test the AI tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ask someone younger. Honestly, I'd say no politely. Let the day staff find the bugs first.

say: **We'll see**, since many tools are announced and never used.
He doesn't care as long as it doesn't slow the **drug round**.
think: Night nursing is **hands and eyes**, so AI barely touches him.
The worry is losing the **night healthcare assistant**.

Keeps saving but **holds off buying** the flat for a year.
Asks Ines how online booking affects **her salon**.
feel: **Uneasy**, because the ward around him changes even if his job doesn't.
S1.quote: A mortgage is twenty-five years, and I don't know what twenty-five years looks like anymore.
fieldNote: Shows **resistant** instinct: delay, wait, let others test first.
Worries about **support staff cuts** more than nurse cuts.
Postponing the **flat purchase** is his main concrete change.

steps.text: Do the AI charting training only when it's compulsory
Keep saving three hundred a month but delay buying for a year
Keep the deposit savings growing in the same account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening, but sick people still need someone in the room. At work I'd say keep calm, we're the last ones they'll replace. I probably wouldn't say much else, I'm not a speeches person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two years is too fast for me. I'm not good with new things. The thinking part of my job, the charts, the handover notes, the bed requests, goes in 2028, and then by 2031 the robots come for the washes and turns, and I'd be thirty-one and only know one thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the flat plan completely and keep the deposit money as an emergency fund. I'd take every extra night shift I could get for those first years, to build up the pot. And I'd ask Ines whether hairdressing, which robots will struggle with, could be our backup income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, properly. I'd probably go quiet for a while, which is what I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robots come about three years after the thinking AI. What does that gap mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep my job for maybe three more years while everyone around me in offices loses theirs. Being the safe one for a bit is strange. I'd use those years to save, because after that I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retrain into something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't know what into. If AI does all the thinking work, there's no desk job to retrain for. I'd probably stay a nurse as long as anyone would pay me, and then see.

say: It's frightening, but sick people still need **someone in the room**.
Colleagues should keep calm, because nurses are **the last ones** replaced.
think: Two years is **too fast** for someone slow with new things.
By **2031** robots take washes and turns, leaving him with one skill.
do: Stops the flat plan and keeps the deposit as an **emergency fund**.
Takes **extra night shifts** to build up the pot.
Talks with Ines about **her hairdressing** as a backup income.
feel: Properly **worried**, likely to go quiet for a while.
S2.quote: I keep my job for maybe three more years while everyone around me in offices loses theirs. Being the safe one for a bit is strange.
fieldNote: Sees the **three-year gap** as a strange window of safety.
No retraining idea, since **desk work** would also be gone.
Leans on **Ines's hands-on trade** as a household backup.
Retreats into **silence** under stress, by his own account.

steps.text: Turn the flat deposit into an emergency fund
Pick up every extra night shift offered for three years
Cancel the plan to buy a flat with Ines

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is something, at least. People can get ready. At work I'd say the same as always: we're needed until we're not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd spend the first couple of years waiting to see if it's real. That's just me. Once it gets closer, around 2030, I'd start worrying properly about 2034 when the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep saving for the deposit but not buy until I saw what happened. I'd maybe do one course, like the tissue viability one, because wound care is fiddly and hands-on. And I'd keep the notebook, obviously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious underneath, calm on top. That's how I'd be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait two years. What would you be watching for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the day staff stop writing their own notes. If I come in at seven and the handover is all written by a machine, I'll know AGI is real. And whether the hospital stops hiring healthcare assistants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ines say about the waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ines would tell me to stop thinking about it and book the holiday. She's better at living than me. But she'd also ask what we'd do in 2034, and I wouldn't have an answer.

say: Five years is **something**, at least, so people can get ready.
His line at work stays the same: nurses are **needed until they're not**.
think: He'd spend **two years waiting** to see if it's real.
Around **2030** he'd start worrying properly about robots in 2034.
do: Keeps saving but **doesn't buy** until things are clearer.
Takes the **tissue viability course**, since wound care is hands-on.
S3.quote: If I come in at seven and the handover is all written by a machine, I'll know AGI is real.
fieldNote: His signal is a **machine-written handover**, a very concrete marker.
Picks a **hands-on specialism** as his one small move.

steps.text: Wait two years before deciding anything about the flat
Take the tissue viability course on wound care
Keep saving three hundred a month for the deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, lots can happen. I wouldn't say much more. At the station I'd say let's worry about this year's rota first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years means I can mostly ignore it for now. By 2039 I'd be thirty-nine, maybe a charge nurse on nights. That's a long way off, and nursing will still need people for a lot of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the flat with Ines next year as planned. I'd keep my nights. I might try the AI charting once the day staff have been using it for a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Ten years is too far for me to worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of that decade you'd plan for now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a bit more saving after we buy, a pension top-up. My dad never planned and he's working at sixty-three. I don't want that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd try the charting in a couple of years. What would change your mind sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Ruth (the nurse who trained me) started using it, I'd try it. She's even more stubborn than me, so if she's using it, it works.

At the station he'd say worry about **this year's rota** first.
think: Ten years means he can **mostly ignore** it for now.
By **2039** he might be a charge nurse on nights.
do: Buys the **flat with Ines** next year as planned.
Keeps his **nights** and tries AI charting after others do.
Adds a **pension top-up** after the purchase.
feel: **Calm**, because ten years feels too far away to worry about.
S4.quote: My dad never planned and he's working at sixty-three. I don't want that.
fieldNote: A decade lets him **return to normal plans**, including the flat.

Motivated by his **father's lack of planning**.

steps.text: Buy the flat with Ines next year as planned
Keep working nights on the medical ward
Start a small pension top-up after buying the flat

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'm slow, and two years doesn't give slow people a chance. What would help is knowing the hospital won't cut the night staff, and maybe some help with house deposits so we're not stuck renting when it all changes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Nights. Nobody thinks about night staff. If robots come, the hospital will try them on nights first, because there are fewer people to complain. That's my guess anyway.

headlineQuote: If robots come, the hospital will try them on nights first, because there are fewer people to complain.
portrait: Victor is a **27-year-old night nurse** on a general medical ward who keeps patient numbers in a paper notebook.
He never uses AI and prefers to **wait** until others have tested anything new.
He and his girlfriend Ines, a hairdresser, are **saving for a flat** deposit.
He's **calm** with lots of time and **anxious** when AGI comes fast, mostly about having one skill.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years gives slow movers no chance.
whatWouldHelp: A promise that **night staffing** won't be cut, and **deposit help** for first-time buyers.
